# Interactive WebGPU Plush Cow Material Study ![Preview by @vib3coded](<../data/gifs/2108572856044986846.gif>) By [@vib3coded]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — XPBD: Name the physics model or simulation type, then check parameters, stability and interaction response. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Cow" in the same studio style as my previous plush toys (plush goat / crab / shark / penguin): editorial layout, large italic serif title "Plush / Cow.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 029", live status chip, specimen panel with tools and sliders, stats row (Mass, Volume, Steps, Moos), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile (no horizontal scroll). The toy: a round stuffed Holstein cow (inspired by the cartoon cow that runs on its udder) who stands and runs on the four teats of her big pink udder — the splayed teats are her only legs. Body = one smooth SDF (round barrel body, big head, wide hot-pink muzzle, rounded udder with a crease, four teats ending in felt pads, a rope tail with a black shaggy tuft) meshed with surface nets. Black Holstein spots with wobbly edges (one around an eye), glossy button eyes, stubby cream felt horns, embroidered oval nostrils and a smile, pink blush, and two cloth ears sewn on sticking straight out at the sides (white outside, pink inside) that flap like wings. Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, volume readout ~100%), skinned to the mesh. Posture-driven locomotion: teat nodes are feet with footing targets, swing lift and a lead point; trot in diagonal pairs (front-left + back-right, then the others). Behaviours: Trot (wanders), Gallop (bouncy laps), Hop (airborne, ears beat like wings), Moo (WebAudio low sawtooth "mmm-OOO" through an opening/closing lowpass, ears flick up, slow head toss), Topple (falls on her side and rocks back up), Smooth fur, Reset. Booping her nose with the finger makes her moo. Fur: real-time shell fur with per-vertex pile (soft coat, short head, velvety pink muzzle and udder, long tail tuft and forelock), combable with the Comb tool. Tools: Hand (grab & squash, pull ears), Finger (poke / she follows it), Comb. Sliders: Stuffing, Pile (mm), Table friction (felt ↔️ ice). Palettes: Holstein, Jersey, Strawberry. 60 fps. ``` ☆ Found this useful? [Identity Lock | Man] Adult male, ~30, short dark brown hair, light stubble, light olive skin; navy jacket, grey hoodie, dark jeans; holding two white paper coffee cups without logos; continuous single actor, no face-swapping or outfit changes. [Space] Fixed geography: ~15m wide two-lane urban street flanked by storefronts; warm-lit cafe on left with glass door facing street; glass bus stop on right facing cafe; street extends to horizon; meteor streaks from top right to horizon, exploding outside city; dust wall surges towards camera; he exits cafe on left, she waits at bus stop on right, meeting in street center without screen direction inversion; ~10 pedestrians. [First Frame] 24mm low-angle wide shot looking down street; quiet night street, shop lights, streetlamps, dark sky; top-right sky glows bright orange-white. [Timeline / SHOT 1] 0.0–4.0s | 24mm low wide upward tilt: 0.0–1.5s sky lights up brighter than day, cast shadows swing rapidly; 1.5–3.0s pedestrians gaze up as massive burning meteor streaks across top-right sky towards horizon; 3.0–4.0s meteor glare reflects on cafe door glass, creating first match cut. [Timeline / SHOT 2] 4.0–9.0s | Match cut from glare, 35mm handheld outside cafe: 4.0–5.5s he pushes door open holding two coffees, looks up and halts; 5.5–7.0s he sees her across the street at the bus stop, eyes meet; 7.0–8.0s both sprint into street; 8.0–9.0s massive white explosion at horizon washes out screen, creating second match cut. [Timeline / SHOT 3] 9.0–15.0s | Match cut from whiteout, 35mm elevated street view: 9.0–11.0s whiteout fades to mushroom cloud and orange fireball; 11.0–13.5s shockwave blasts storefront windows successively towards camera, alarms blare, dust wall rolls forward; both sprint towards street center; 13.5–15.0s nearest window shatters toward lens, creating third match cut. [Timeline / SHOT 4] 15.0–19.0s | Match cut from flying glass, 50mm eye-level profile, both in street center: 15.0–17.0s reaching out, he drops both coffees, liquid spills, glass whirls, dust wall 20m away, wind pulls hair; 17.0s time abruptly freezes completely; 17.0–19.0s absolute standstill except she slowly blinks, creating fourth match cut. [Timeline / SHOT 5] 19.0–25.0s | Match cut from blink, 35mm handheld over her right shoulder: 19.0–20.5s realizing she can move, she looks around; 20.5–23.5s steps forward through suspended shards, gently deflects a floating glass shard which stays in place; passes frozen coffee spill, frozen pigeon, frozen pedestrians, frozen fiery dust wall; 23.5–25.0s approaches him and reaches out, creating fifth match cut. [Timeline / SHOT 6] 25.0–30.0s | Match cut from reaching hand, 50mm close profile: 25.0–26.5s fingertips touch his frozen cheek; 26.5–28.0s he blinks, inhales, looks at her and unfreezes, clasping her hand; 28.0–30.0s adjacent suspended glass shard vibrates and drops; both watch it fall; scene cuts mid-fall. [Physics] Meteor illumination realistically shifts street shadows; shockwave shatters glass sequentially outward; dust wall is volumetric fire/dust; time freeze is total for all background elements with zero motion blur or drift; deflected shard stays at new position; gravity resumes on moving subjects; only final shard vibrates and drops. [Cinematography] 6 sequential camera setups; 5 match cuts matched to ending elements (reflection, flash, shard, blink, hand); camera static during freeze except Shot 5 tracking; no slow motion, no hero low-angles. [Lighting/Color] Opens cold blue with warm shop light; switches to harsh orange-white under meteor; orange-red explosion lighting; frozen world back-lit by fire inside dust wall; red coat remains focal point. [Audio] Shot 1 quiet traffic to escalating roar; Shot 2 doorbell, footsteps, distant impact; Shot 3 blast roar, shattering windows, alarms; Shot 4 wind/glass noise abruptly cuts to dead silence at 17s; Shot 5 quiet footsteps on glass and soft breath; Shot 6 sharp inhale and gentle glass hum. [Locks] Strictly 6 shots, 5 match cuts; zero spoken dialogue; continuous outfits and character identities without fusion; exact anatomical consistency; live-action film realism; video cuts while the shard falls. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Interactive Three.js Newton's Cradle ![Preview by @ivanainai](<../data/gifs/2108625335122026542.gif>) By [@ivanainai]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — fixed camera: Lock the camera to reduce framing drift and make subject motion easier to inspect. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a complete, single-file HTML/Three.js experience showing an exceptionally beautiful, interactive Newton’s cradle. Use the attached image as the reference for the recognizable construction: five polished metal balls suspended inside two parallel chrome frames. The result should feel like a luxury product filmed in a real photography studio, with convincing materials, graceful pendulum motion, and working collision physics. Open directly into the finished scene. The first rendered frame must already be composed beautifully enough to use as a video thumbnail. Prioritize three things equally: the beauty of the chrome, the physical construction, and the correctness of the motion. Create a square, recording-ready composition that adapts to the browser without stretching. Center one substantial Newton’s cradle on a seamless warm-ivory studio surface. Use a fixed camera positioned mostly in front of the cradle, slightly above the balls and slightly off-center. Show enough depth to distinguish the front and rear frames, while keeping all five balls easy to count. Use a restrained product-photography perspective, approximately equivalent to a 70mm lens. Avoid a wide-angle appearance. The cradle should fill most of the image. Leave comfortable margins for the full outward swing on both sides. Neither the balls nor the frame may leave the image during normal operation. Keep the camera stationary throughout. No orbiting, automatic zoom, camera shake, or cuts. Construct exactly five identical, perfectly round polished stainless-steel spheres. At rest, their centers must form one horizontal row, with neighboring spheres touching. Their diameters, masses, and suspension lengths must match. Use two slender, parallel, inverted-U chrome support frames with rounded corners, positioned in front of and behind the ball row. Each ball must hang from two fine, taut suspension wires: one connected to the front support and one to the rear support. These wires constrain its motion to the shared vertical swing plane. Include small, believable attachment details. The wires must connect visibly to the balls and frame. The support frame and anchors remain completely stationary. Update the suspension geometry from the actual ball positions every frame. Wires must never stretch, disconnect, pass through the spheres, or wave independently. Choose elegant proportions: substantial spheres, slender tubular supports, and enough suspension length for a satisfying swing. Avoid thick ropes, oversized frames, and a bulky decorative base. Make the metal look convincingly reflective. Use physically based metallic materials, high-quality sphere geometry, restrained surface roughness, and a carefully designed reflection environment. Create large studio-softbox reflections that wrap naturally around the spheres and curved frame. Include broad bright highlights, darker reflected regions, and subtle warm tones from the studio. The spheres must retain readable volume. Avoid flat gray metal, featureless white balls, plastic shading, and excessive bloom. Build the reflection environment procedurally inside the file. Do not depend on downloaded HDR images or external texture assets. Use a large soft key light from the upper-left, gentle fill from the opposite side, and a restrained rim light to define the metal against the background. Add soft contact shadows beneath the frame and moving shadows beneath the balls. Shadows should follow the motion and help communicate height. Keep the background uncluttered, with a very subtle ivory gradient. The overall image should feel calm, precise, and expensive. Implement a working simplified Newton’s cradle simulation. Represent each sphere as an equal-mass pendulum with an angular position and angular velocity. Gravity must drive the swing. Derive the sphere positions from the pendulum geometry. Use stable time integration and collision handling that can propagate impacts through the full chain of touching balls. A fixed timestep with sufficient substeps, event-based impacts, or a suitable constraint-aware solver is acceptable. Choose an approach that remains stable at different rendering frame rates. Do not animate the balls with unrelated sine waves or a prerecorded sequence. The motion must respond to the simulated state and user input. The required behavior is: Release one outer ball. It swings into the row, transfers its motion through the chain, and approximately one ball swings outward at the opposite end. The outgoing ball returns, strikes the row, and sends the original outer ball outward again. Release two adjacent balls together from one side. Approximately two balls must swing outward together from the opposite side. The remaining balls should stay close to their resting positions, allowing small physically plausible movement during impacts. Motion transfers at contact. The outgoing balls must not begin swinging before the incoming balls reach the row. Handle the chain of contacts consistently. A single order-dependent collision pass must not produce a different result when the direction reverses. Collisions should approximately conserve momentum and kinetic energy over the brief impact interval, with small losses. Use gentle damping so the swing amplitude decreases gradually. The simulation must not gain energy, accelerate indefinitely, visibly interpenetrate, jitter continuously, or send the entire row swinging after every impact. The balls should accelerate toward the bottom of their arcs and slow naturally near their turning points. Avoid constant-speed swinging. Start with the leftmost ball raised approximately 35 degrees and the other four hanging at rest. Hold this initial pose briefly, around 0.4 seconds, then release automatically. The experience must immediately demonstrate the classic alternating motion without requiring a click. Continue running without an automatic reset. Add a small, elegant control strip near the bottom edge with: “1 BALL” “2 BALLS” Pause / Resume Reset “0.25×” slow motion Keep these controls visually secondary. They must not overlap the cradle or its swing paths. Selecting “1 BALL” or “2 BALLS” should reset the simulation, raise the corresponding leftmost ball or pair to the same release angle, briefly hold, and release. Reset should restore and replay the currently selected mode. Slow motion must scale simulated time while preserving the same physics. It must not change gravity, collision behavior, or suspension geometry. Allow the user to drag either outer ball outward within its permitted swing plane, then release it. Clamp the drag angle to a sensible maximum, around 45 degrees. Keep its suspension wires taut throughout. Add an “H” keyboard shortcut to hide or reveal the controls for clean recording. Keep the experience silent. No music, collision sounds, particles, motion trails, impact flashes, explanatory overlays, large titles, model names, or decorative text. Deliver one complete HTML file with inline CSS and JavaScript. Use one consistently pinned Three.js version and matching modules if needed. No build step, backend, external models, external textures, or HDR downloads. Initialize the renderer, camera, lighting, materials, and starting pose before revealing the canvas. Avoid a visible black startup frame. Support browser resizing without distorting the scene. Aim for smooth performance on a normal laptop and cap pixel density sensibly. Before finishing, check that: Exactly five spheres remain visible and correctly suspended. The complete frame and maximum swing fit inside the square composition. One-ball mode transfers approximately one ball at each impact. Two-ball mode transfers approximately two balls at each impact. Pause, reset, slow motion, and dragging work. Chrome reflections remain readable throughout the motion. The scene appears immediately and produces no runtime errors. Return the complete working HTML. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # First-Person 3D Procedural Arms and Dynamic Grip Rigging in Three.js ![Preview by @maxt3chno](<../data/gifs/2108637690698633713.gif>) By [@maxt3chno]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — Three.js: Name the implementation or rendering tool and prepare its environment; a tool name alone is not a complete workflow. ## Prompt (English) ```text TASK: Build production-grade first-person arms ("Hands 2.0") for a Three.js browser game, then fix them until every pose actually holds the object it should hold. Do the whole thing yourself with scripts, from generating the model to the in-game checks. I already did this once. Below is what works and the traps I fell into, so you don't repeat them. ━━━ PART 1 — THE MODEL (Blender + MPFB2, fully scripted) ━━━ 1. Don't patch AI-generated "statue" arms (Meshy etc.). Chaotic topology with no edge loops at the joints and fingers baked into a pose will crease at every bend. Without clavicle and twist bones the wrist twists like a candy wrapper. Gluing separate generated parts together only adds seams to the same bad mesh. Start over with a real humanoid generator. 2. Use Blender (headless: `blender --background --python tools/hands/*.py`) + MPFB2 (MakeHuman, CC0) and its official asset packs. Put every step in a script so it can be rebuilt: - build_body.py: macro params (male, ~30 y/o, wiry and lean: muscle ~0.66, weight ~0.3) plus local arm targets. - build_arms.py: game skeleton with clavicle → shoulder → upperarm01/02 → lowerarm01/02 (twist bones!) → wrist → metacarpals → 3 phalanges per finger. Keep skin only from the elbow down and apply subdiv 1. Make the sleeve a separate mesh on the same bones, with real geometry for the rolled cuff. Accessories (watch, bracelet) are parented to forearm/wrist bones; watch hands are bones too. - build_tex.py: UVs, then bake veins, tendons and knuckles into geometry and normals. Author every detail in bone-local 3D space so it survives re-UVs, then bake in Cycles. - https://t.co/3ocKmFbTLm → pack script → hands_v2.glb. Budget ~25–40k tris for both arms incl. sleeves (they're huge on screen), 1–2 skin materials + sleeve + accessories. Textures 2048² on High, 1024² on Low, plus a tiling micro-normal for pores. - Generate a full body with pants, boots and the same shirt, and save it as a .blend for a future "player body" stage. Don't put it in the game yet. 3. Look: tanned back of hand and forearm, paler palm and inner side. Scars, calluses, short nails with natural cuticles. Flannel sleeves rolled just below the elbow, with a visible inside-out lining on the roll. Tactical watch on the left wrist, cord bracelet on the right. 4. Check skin weights on stress poses before you export: fist, pinch, spread fingers, 90° supination. Fix weights in a script, not by hand. 5. HARD STOP #1: render review shots in Blender (neutral light and warm daylight): front, back, palms, fist, pinch, cylinder grip, spread fingers, sleeve close-up, two plaid colour variants. Wait for my verbal OK. Iterate. Don't integrate anything into the game until I say yes. 6. glTF only gives you standard material slots, so use them as carriers. Example: MR = (R AO, G roughness, B subsurface thickness), emissive = masks (R hair, G dirt accumulation order), clearcoatNormal = pore tile. Document the mapping and read it back in the runtime. ━━━ PART 2 — SHADERS (MeshStandard/Physical + onBeforeCompile) ━━━ - Skin: wrap lighting, back-lit translucency in thin areas (fingers, webbing, knuckles go red against the sun), pore detail normal, micro-sheen, tan gradient by mask. - Hair: 4 fur shells in ONE instanced draw, only on hairy triangles, visible on the silhouette against the sun. Disabled on Low. - Dynamic state: · wet = max(world wetness, rain when not under a roof), with two layers of droplets. The sleeve goes darker when wet. · dirt builds up from game events (gather, pickup, log, fish_land, climb_out…), fingers and palms first through the mask, and washes off in water or rain. - Arm lighting mirrors the world: shade under roofs, lamp light, lightning. - Precompile every arm shader behind the loading screen. https://t.co/nXMh9v1zBi.programs.length must not grow during gameplay. - Budget: the arm overlay may cost at most ~0.3 ms more GPU than before on High. Measure with a timer query before and after, not by feel. ━━━ PART 3 — THE ARM SYSTEM (data, not code) ━━━ Goal: a new item or action (axe, bow, paddle, steering wheel) should be a data entry plus a clip, never new logic. 1. Rig wrapper: bone map, wrist twist spread over the twist bones (e.g. 0.3 / 0.8 on lowerarm01/02). No candy-wrapper wrists. 2. Two-bone IK (shoulder–elbow–wrist) with pole vectors (elbows down and out) and joint limits. 3. grips.js: for each item, per hand: `at / axis / back / r / diag / gap / slide / fingers / thumb` in item space. One hand owns the item, the other IKs to its socket. 4. Fingers are always a joint table `[[mcp, pip, dip, spread, twist] × 5]` (absolute bend) and blend between poses. Autogrip closes the fingers until they touch the handle. 5. Animation layers, in this order: base pose → clip keyframes → IK → procedural (breath, bob, mouse-turn inertia, sway, recoil, fatigue tremor) → additive reactions. Smooth transitions between states. 6. Clips: JSON keyframes in code, plus importing .glb animations (with empty hand_R/hand_L) for future Blender-made actions. Clip events (strike frame, bow release) go onto the effects bus. 7. In-game pose editor (Shift+H, game keeps running, cursor free): sliders for item offset and rotation, sockets, every finger joint, elbow pole, shoulders, layer speeds. Show changes live. "Copy" puts JSON on the clipboard to paste into grips.js. I need to be able to tune a grip without Blender. 8. Keep the old public API as a facade (hands.anim, reach, lampInHand…) so fishing, boat, lamp, weapons, sleep and the seaplane don't need deep rewrites. 9. Port EVERY existing action: rifle (stance, ADS, fire, reload with mag, dry fire), knife (2 strikes), stone throw, fishing rod (cast, fight, reel, fish in hand), carried log, lamp, reach and pickup, plant gathering, inspect, crate, swimming (breaststroke and crawl), boat tiller, hands down while sleeping, hidden arms in vehicles. Each one must be at least as good as before. Delete the old arm code only after everything is ported (keep a backup). 10. HARD STOP #2: in-game screenshots for my approval (idle, rifle, rod, log, lamp at night, wet after swimming, dirty after firewood, under a roof and in full sun). ━━━ PART 4 — THE FIX PASS (bake this in from day one) ━━━ The first version shipped with these bugs. Every one of them came from old poses written for "stump" arms with no shoulder. ROOT CAUSE: a real arm has a fixed length (shoulder→wrist ≈ 0.48 m in view space). Old poses put wrists at targets the arm can't reach. The solver then "cheated": it pushed the clavicle out (up to 0.32 m) and clamped the wrist rotation. The hand ended up somewhere else, while finger curls were cached for the ideal hand position, so the fingers squeezed thin air. - Rifle, left hand: handguard 0.516 m away with a 0.479 m arm → shoulder pushed out ~0.3 m and the fist still sat 3.8 cm below the handguard. - Rifle, right hand: wrist rotation clamped by ~21°, palm not seated on the grip. FIXES, as SYSTEM features: 1. Shoulder stance as data: per item/pose, `stance: { L:[x,y,z], R:[x,y,z] }` with smooth blending, and the elbow pole moves with the shoulder. Rifle: left shoulder forward and in, right shoulder slightly back (a real shooter's torso rotation). The left elbow stays slightly bent and the clavicle doesn't stretch. 2. Elbow auto-swivel: give each forearm a pronation range (e.g. R −100°…+95°, 0 = thumb up). If the requested pole would over-twist the forearm or bend the wrist past its limit, rotate the elbow around the shoulder–wrist line to the nearest valid angle. The old poses were silently over-twisted (+101° on the rifle, +80° on the knife). 3. Grip by the REAL handle shape. A cylinder radius is wrong: the knife handle was a 2.6 × 4.2 cm oval, not Ø2.5 cm, so the knuckles sank 2–6 mm into it. - Handle = elliptical cylinder with end caps (`sec` [along back, across], `span`, `inset`). - measureSection(item, socket): take the cross-section automatically by slicing the item mesh around `at` along `axis`. - CPU-skin the hand (SkinnedMesh.getVertexPosition, palm and phalanx vertices with weights) and test real skin vertices, not phalanx tips. - gripFit, cached and computed at startup: first push the palm out until it leaves the handle. Then close each finger with all joints together until first contact, and after that only the joints past the touching phalanx. If the start pose already intersects, open it up. - Fingertip targets: `fingers: {1: {to:[x,y,z]}}` puts the index pad on the trigger. 4. Validator: hands.check(pose) and hands.checkAll(). Run every scenario × both hands + the live rod pose, print a console table, and show it live in the Shift+H editor with a "Check all poses" button. RED if wrist miss > 0.5 cm, rotation clamp > 3°, shoulder push > 0.5 cm, twist over the limit > 3°, or any skin vertex deeper than 1.5 mm inside the handle. Don't call the work done until it's all green (mine ended at 122/122). DATA FIXES that came from my screenshots: - Rifle: left hand on the WOODEN handguard, not the metal in front of it. Handguard runs diagonally across the palm, thumb along the left side, forearm coming in from the lower-left corner. Right hand fully on the pistol grip using the grip's real rake (axis (0, 0.95, −0.32), not a guessed 40°), index on the trigger. On reload the hand leads and the mag rides in the hand, and the shoulder dips to follow it. Check sprint, recoil, dry fire, and steering a boat while holding the rifle. - Log: nobody carries a 44 × 7 cm log with two arms like a crate. One hand, an ordinary hammer grip like a bottle: knuckles up, thumb on top, held about a third from the back end, log pointing forward and up from the thumb side, riding in the fist. The throw is a one-handed wind-up and lunge. The left hand stays free, so the lamp stays in it. - Swimming: fingers together and slightly cupped (no fan), hands in the bottom third of the frame. Crawl recovery comes in from the side, palm facing out. The sleeve never covers the middle of the screen and the palm never faces the camera. - Fix every pose the validator flags: stone wind-up and throw, aim, lamp, lamp lowered, climbing, reach. ━━━ RULES ━━━ - Backup before each stage. Measure, don't guess: write every claim down as a number (cm, °, ms, tris, programs). - No performance regression: grip fit is cached per socket, and the validator only runs in the editor or dev builds. - Write down what's still unfinished honestly in the report (e.g. "right hand mostly below the frame on the rifle", "pinky sometimes curls without contact"). - DONE = I approved the renders and the screenshots, bends are clean on every grip, fingers wrap handles with zero penetrations, wet and dirt work, every old action works on the new system, a new item is one grips.js entry + one clip, and FPS is unchanged. ``` ☆ Found this useful? The stack of glass elements in their groups, the aperture blades that open and close, the focus motor, the image stabilizer, the zoom cams, and the gold contacts on the mount. # WebGPU Plush Marlin Interactive Study ![Preview by @vib3coded](<../data/gifs/2108850731750940711.gif>) By [@vib3coded]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — XPBD: Name the physics model or simulation type, then check parameters, stability and interaction response. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Marlin" in the same studio style as my plush hammerhead / plush shark: editorial layout, italic serif title "Plush / Marlin.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 030", live status chip, specimen panel (tools, fur palettes, sliders, action buttons), stats row (Mass, Volume, Beat, Fish eaten), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile. The toy: a plush blue marlin, normal and realistic in proportion (not a meme). One SDF body meshed with surface nets: a long fusiform body, deep behind the head and slender at the tail stock, laterally compressed; a long tapering felt bill (spear) from the upper jaw, slightly upturned; a tall sail-like first dorsal fin raked back from a high peak over the head and running low down the back; a small second dorsal and anal fin; long narrow scythe pectorals and thin pelvic fins; a tall crescent (lunate) tail with the notch scooped out; big glass eyes; a small mouth slit under the bill with a lower jaw that swings open on a hinge. Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tet volume preservation), skinned to the mesh. It swims with a stiff travelling wave mostly in its back third, circles, banks into turns. CONCEPT A translucent, wobbly jelly cube floats in the middle of the page like a collectible diorama. Inside the top layer lives a tiny prehistoric island: a lush jungle of palms and giant ferns, a smoking volcano, a baby T-Rex, a long-neck brontosaurus, a few eggs in a nest and a fossil skull half buried in the sand. Below the island the cube shows cut-away soil layers (sand, clay, dark rock, glowing magma at the very bottom) like a cake slice. LOOK - Soft, warm off-white studio background, huge soft shadow under the cube, no harsh black. - The jelly must feel real: transmission/refraction, thickness, subtle caustics, slight inner glow, glossy rim highlight, gentle subsurface colour. - Editorial typography on the left: big italic serif title "Dino Jelly." with a one-line subtitle, small caps captions in the bottom corners. - A minimal frosted control panel on the right, tiny type, 1px borders, lots of air. MOTION - The cube idles with a slow float and a continuous jelly wobble (spring-damped vertex deformation). Clicking/dragging the cube pokes it and the whole thing jiggles, the island inside lags behind slightly. - Volcano emits smoke puffs and occasional lava bombs that splash into the jelly with ripples. - The T-Rex blinks and roars every few seconds (head tilt + jelly ripple); the brontosaurus slowly turns its neck; palms sway. - Camera: slow orbit, OrbitControls ``` ☆ Found this useful? Make it beautiful, use lots of tokens, iterate until you're genuinely proud. No external assets — draw everything in code (SVG/canvas/CSS). It should just run. # Thermal Courier: Dawn Balloon Mail Run Canvas Game & Trailer ![Preview by @jeffbruchado](<../data/gifs/2108951077991362922.gif>) By [@jeffbruchado]() · **Prompt fragment** — the shared text may need additional instructions. > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — single self-contained HTML file: Specify one HTML deliverable for easy browser playback; still check whether the implementation loads external dependencies. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a single self-contained HTML file (canvas, no libraries, no network, no audio) for a 1280x720 landscape game, scaled to fit, where the player flies a striped hot air balloon over endless desert mesas at dawn and drops a hanging mail sack onto glowing landing pads atop mesa towers. Controls: hold Space or touch to fire the burner, hold Down or a second touch zone to open the vent, release key or double tap to drop the sack; there is no horizontal thrust, so the only way to steer is to climb or sink into one of 5 stacked wind bands, each with its own speed between -90 and +90 px/s that slowly drifts every 20 seconds. Buoyancy simulation: envelope temperature eases toward the burner target with a 1.8 s time constant, lift is proportional to envelope temperature minus an ambient temperature that falls with altitude, propane burns at 6 percent per second of burner use, and the balloon has real momentum, so good players plan climbs early. Make the wind visible with 600 streak particles advected through the band field plus curl noise turbulence, drawn as fading 8 frame trails, and with cloth flags on every tower that point the local wind. The mail sack hangs on a 12 segment Verlet rope solved with 8 constraint iterations per frame at a fixed 120 Hz substep; it must swing with the balloon's acceleration, never stretch or explode, collide with the mesa terrain polygons, and score only if it comes to rest on a pad (3 rings of accuracy). Procedural world: a seeded generator builds an endless skyline of flat-topped mesas, arches and spires in 3 parallax layers, placing 1 pad tower every 900 to 1400 px so pads always sit within reach of at least 2 wind bands. Camera follows with velocity lookahead and eases its zoom from 1.0 to 0.8 as the balloon climbs.… ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Three.js 徒步探险纪实 3D 场景与解说视频生成 ![Preview by @shengtang135754](<../data/gifs/2109132993617125532.gif>) By [@shengtang135754]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — single-file HTML: Specify one HTML deliverable for easy browser playback; still check whether the implementation loads external dependencies. ## Prompt (English) ```text Please use Three.js to write a single-file HTML (index.html) to create a "hiking documentary style" 3D scene for screen recording narration videos. [Basic Requirements] - Import Three.js via CDN (cdnjs or jsdelivr), no build tools required, runnable directly by double-clicking in a browser. - Strict 16:9 aspect ratio, designed internally at 1920x1080, centered with aspect ratio maintained and black bars filled when resizing. - All adjustable parameters (terrain seed, route points, camera speed, etc.) centralized in a CONFIG object at top of file. [Terrain] - Use multi-layer noise (Simplex/Perlin, self-implemented) to generate a north-south mountain gorge: high mountains on both sides, valley bottom in the middle with a winding riverbed. - Color by elevation and slope: deep brown/gray ridges, earthy yellow slopes, light yellow valley, blue-gray riverbed, light snow on peaks. - Add fog and directional light to create a cold, dry plateau atmosphere. [Route & Character] - Define hiking route using a list of (x, z) waypoints in CONFIG, smooth with CatmullRomCurve3 matching terrain height. - Render route as thick red line (subtle glow), passed section bright red, upcoming section semi-transparent. - Red low-poly figure (capsule + sphere head + red coat) walking along route at constant speed, adjustable speed, supports pause. - Support event markers on route (e.g., Assembly point, Last seen), displayed as vertical signs with text or pulsing rings. [Camera] - Four modes switchable via keys 1-4 with smooth transitions: 1. High overhead view (flying forward along route, slightly tilted) 2. Follow (behind and above character) 3. Orbit (slow orbit around character) 4. Free look (drag to rotate, scroll zoom, WASD move) - Camera speed, height, pitch angle adjustable in CONFIG. [UI Overlay (HTML/CSS)] - Columns of member cards on both sides: square avatar (solid color + initial placeholder, customizable via URL), name, role caption. - Member status: Normal / Deceased (gray card with red border) / Missing (semi-transparent with question mark). - Centered bottom subtitle bar, white text with black stroke, supports [[keyword]] yellow highlight. - Top right shows "Episode X" title and progress bar (optional). [Timeline Driven] - Describe storyline in CONFIG with a TIMELINE array, each entry containing time (seconds) and action: { time: 0, action: "camera", mode: 1 } { time: 3, action: "subtitle", text: "Then why did you dare to [[join]]?", duration: 4 } { time: 8, action: "walk", from: 0, to: 0.4 } { time: 15, action: "status", member: "Hu Yanglin", state: "missing" } { time: 20, action: "marker", at: 0.6, text: "Last seen" } - Playback logic: Space to play/pause, R to reset, auto-trigger events at timestamps. - Small debug panel top-left, press H to hide for clean recording. [Sample Content] - Preset 8 fictional members (Tie Gao - organizer, Qian Niao, Hu Yanglin, Mimi, Members 5-8), ~90s demo timeline covering overhead view, walking, event markers, status changes, ending subtitles. [Code Requirements] - Clearly partitioned code with Chinese comments (terrain, route, character, camera, UI, timeline). - Stable 30fps+ on standard laptops, terrain resolution ~256x256 vertices. - Explain how to modify route, avatars, and add timeline events after completion. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Interactive WebGPU Plush Hedgehog Simulation ![Preview by @N1njaCodex](<../data/gifs/2109259805638455401.gif>) By [@N1njaCodex]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — XPBD: Name the physics model or simulation type, then check parameters, stability and interaction response. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Hedgehog" in my plush studio style: editorial layout, large italic serif title "Plush / Hedgehog.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 021", caption "A coat of soft felted spines, a button nose, four little paws. Curls up when it is shy.", live status chip, specimen panel on the right (tools, fur palettes, sliders, action buttons), stats row (Mass, Volume, Steps, Curls), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile. The toy: a round plush hedgehog — one SDF body (a round bun with a pointed snout, two little round ears, a flat seat) meshed with surface nets, a button nose, glass eyes, four short plush paws (tubes with a bendable wire inside that keep the shape you bend them to). Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, live volume readout), skinned to the mesh, sitting under gravity on Coulomb friction. It breathes with its flanks, twitches its snout when it sniffs, and slowly rights itself toward the way it last walked. Curling into a ball is a second rest shape found once at load (the body led nose-to-tail and squeezed into a sphere so the stuffing can really take that shape); curling blends every cell's rest shape and every tet's rest volume toward it. Nothing holds the ball upright, so a push makes it roll; when it stops it unrolls and stands up again. Spines: hundreds of soft felted cones rooted on the skin, rebuilt every frame from the skin's stretch and turn; they lie back toward the tail, stand up when it bristles or curls, lag behind every jolt on a damped spring, part around the finger and fold on the table instead of going through it. Cream root, dark band, pale tip, a short fuzz over each. The face, belly and paws wear minky shell fur that lies back from the nose and takes the comb. Behaviours: Trundle (walks on its paws in diagonal pairs), Curl up, Roll, Bristle, Smooth fur, Reset. Hand: pick it up — hold it a moment and it curls into a prickly ball in your hand; put it down, squash it, throw it; bend a paw. Finger: it trundles over and sniffs your finger; run the finger through the spines and they part; poke its back and it huffs and rolls up. Comb: brush the minky. Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Spines. Palettes: Hazel, Ash, Blush. ¼ speed and mesh toggles. 60 fps. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Interactive WebGPU Plush Penguin Simulation with Soft-Body Physics and Shell Fur ![Preview by @vib3coded](<../data/gifs/2109288662319919127.gif>) By [@vib3coded]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — XPBD: Name the physics model or simulation type, then check parameters, stability and interaction response. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Penguin": editorial studio layout, large italic serif title "Plush / Penguin.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 016", caption "A fluffy egg on two felt feet. It waddles, it toboggans, it falls over — and always gets back up.", live status chip, specimen panel on the right, stats row (Mass, Volume, Steps, Slide in cm), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile. The toy: a round plush penguin chick — an egg-shaped stuffed body as one SDF meshed with surface nets, a dark cap and back, a pale fluffy face and belly, big glossy safety-glass eyes, a small felt beak, pink cheeks, two flat felt feet. Its flippers are separate cloth pieces (particle cloth sewn to points embedded in the body) that flop, flap and stretch. Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, live volume readout), skinned to the mesh, standing on a table with Coulomb friction. Locomotion by posture: a weak pull of the whole body toward its rest shape turned to an orientation and carried with its centre of mass, so the stuffing does the moving. Behaviours: Waddle (rocks side to side, lifting each foot and setting it down ahead), Belly slide (a little hop, flops forward onto its tummy and toboggans across the table, then rocks back up), Flap (happy flapping and a couple of hops), Topple (falls onto its back, belly or side and rocks itself upright with an overshoot), Smooth fur, Reset. Finger: it waddles over to your finger; push it and it falls over. Hand: pick it up, squash it, pull a flipper and it comes along. Fur: real-time shell fur with alpha-to-coverage — long fluffy down on the body, short on the face, combable with a Comb tool (against the grain darker, with it shinier). Sliders: Stuffing, Pile (mm), Table (felt ↔ ice friction, so it slides further on ice). Palettes: Chick, Classic, Little blue. ¼ speed and mesh toggles, Pause. 60 fps. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Interactive 3D Hand Gestures with Framer and MediaPipe ![Preview by @emili_iv](<../data/gifs/2109388484569924030.gif>) By [@emili_iv]() · **Prompt fragment** — the shared text may need additional instructions. > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — click: Specify how user input changes state so the result is interactive rather than merely viewable. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a full-screen "Themed Scene" component (1200×1000) with two variants, Light (white background, black lines) and Dark (black background, white lines). It switches between them with a 0.4s ease-in-out tween. Put it on the home page so it fills the width.3D OBJECTS (built from Framer 3D transforms, not images)Each object uses the same three-layer nesting:1. Outer "stage" frame: sets perspective. A hand-tracking override that handles grab, move and scale goes here.2. "Rotation" frame: keeps children in 3D. A hand-tracking override that handles rotation goes here.3. Object frame: keeps children in 3D, with a resting tilt.a) Cube: stage 424×424, perspective 1600px. Rotation frame 300×300, centered. Cluster tilted -28° on X and 36° on Y. Inside it, one 150px cube built from 6 faces with 1.5px black outlines and no fill: front: pushed forward 75px · back: turned 180° on Y and pushed back 75px right: shifted right 75px and turned 90° on Y · left: shifted left 75px and turned -90° on Y top: shifted up 75px and turned 90° on X · bottom: shifted down 75px and turned -90° on Xb) Box: stage 282×282, perspective 1200px. A 120w × 150h × 200d box tilted -22° on X and 38° on Y. Its faces are filled with the variant's background color and outlined, so the box reads as solid.c) Diamond (octahedron wireframe): stage 322×308, perspective 1600px. A 281px object turned -90° on Z. It's made of 12 lines, each 1.5px thick, placed freely and positioned with sideways turns, Z turns and depth offsets so they meet at 6 points. Edges at the back are lighter or https://t.co/nia9sbosrt the three objects loosely across the canvas so they don't overlap.LIGHT SWITCHA 120px-wide vertical stack with 16px rounded corners. It holds an "on" switch drawing, an "off" switch drawing and a label ("Lights on" / "Lights off"). Clicking it toggles the Light and Dark variants. A hand-press override goes on it.HAND TRACKING (one code file: three overrides plus a toggle button)- Toggle button: a pill-shaped "Start hand tracking" / "Stop hand tracking" button centered at the bottom. It starts the webcam and Google MediaPipe hand tracking (two hands, GPU with CPU fallback). A mirrored 240×180 webcam preview sits in the bottom-right corner with the hand skeleton drawn on top. Each hand gets an on-screen cursor: the left hand is a solid dot, the right hand a dashed ring, and the cursor fills in while it's holding or rotating something.- Gestures: • LEFT hand pinch (thumb to index) on an object = grab it. Moving the hand moves the object with a spring. Widening or tightening the pinch scales it (0.25× to 4×). • To let go, open the palm or touch thumb to middle finger. The object then rewinds about 450ms so it doesn't jump at the end. • RIGHT hand pinch on an object = rotate it. Hand movement turns it freely (about one full turn per 500px). Twisting the wrist turns it on the third axis. Rotation is in screen space so turns accumulate without limit and stay smooth at any angle, with no flipping. • Either hand pinching over the light switch = click it.- Make the tracking feel stable: smooth out jitter, use separate thresholds for starting and ending a pinch, and require the fingers to relax before a hand can grab again.- Add an option to swap left and right hands and an option ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Interactive 3D Stained-Glass Hibiscus ![Preview by @ivanainai](<../data/gifs/2109788665899810947.gif>) By [@ivanainai]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — interactive: Specify how user input changes state so the result is interactive rather than merely viewable. ## Prompt (English) ```text Create a beautiful, interactive 3D browser artwork of a single stained-glass hibiscus flower. Use the attached leaf as a reference for material delicacy, intricate veins, translucent colours and restrained presentation. Create an original flower composition. The flower is the entire experience. It fills most of the viewport against a quiet, near-black charcoal background. FLOWER Create five broad, organically shaped petals with gently ruffled edges, subtle asymmetry and graceful curvature. Arrange them into a convincing three-dimensional hibiscus, with natural overlap and a clearly visible centre. Each petal is made from thin, luminous stained glass. Blend ruby pink, coral, pale peach and honey amber within the glass, with delicate marbling and fine branching veins radiating from its base. Use extremely thin antique-gold seams and a finely beveled outer edge. Preserve the delicacy of the glass. Include a slender projecting central column with tiny golden anthers, a gracefully curved stem and two small translucent green leaves. MATERIAL AND LIGHT The glass must have visible thickness, coloured light transmission, subtle surface irregularities and crisp reflections that change with the viewing angle. Overlapping petals should remain readable. Balance illumination so the colours stay luminous and the veins remain visible throughout rotation. Avoid large white reflections that erase the detail. Use soft studio lighting with a warm backlight and a restrained rim light. Avoid excessive bloom, neon colour and heavy black outlines. MOVEMENT AND INTERACTION Start immediately with a flattering three-quarter view. Rotate slowly and smoothly so viewers can inspect the curved petals, thin edges and reverse side. Allow dragging to orbit, scrolling to zoom, and a small pause control. Keep the flower fully framed during automatic rotation. DELIVERY Build actual 3D geometry rendered in the browser. Generate the geometry and textures in code. Deliver a working preview and a downloadable, self-contained stained-glass-flower.html with all dependencies embedded. Run the result, inspect a full rotation, and fix missing surfaces, transparency problems, clipping or washed-out lighting before finishing. Prioritize the quality of the flower over interface decoration. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Torii at High Tide Interactive 3D WebGL Diorama ![Preview by @vib3coded](<../data/gifs/2110014604524896392.gif>) By [@vib3coded]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — fixed 60 Hz: Specify update timing or allocation constraints to reduce stutter; verify performance by running the result. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a single-file interactive WebGL diorama (one index.html, no build step) with Three.js r160 loaded via an import map from https://t.co/lj8MfmK18g, plus OrbitControls and BufferGeometryUtils (mergeVertices, mergeGeometries) from three/examples/jsm. Everything is procedural — no external models or textures. CONCEPT "Torii at High Tide": a miniature Japanese shrine island inspired by Itsukushima, inside a 10×10 block of clear water with rounded edges (vertical corner radius ~0.6, top edge radius ~0.26), on a thin sand-colored base slab, on a warm washi-paper background with a soft floor shadow that fades out with distance (so long dusk shadows never streak across the page). TERRAIN (heightfield ~400×400, clipped to the rounded block, with a boundary "skirt" so the cross-section shows through the water) - Work in a local frame facing the camera (u = across, v = toward the viewer). - A forested dome-shaped hill at the back (~2.4 high), a low sandy shrine terrace at its foot, then a wide, gently sloping tidal flat in front (from ~-0.06 down to ~-0.46), dropping to ~-1.0 at the front and sides. - Two rocky granite headlands framing the bay, each with 1–2 leaning bonsai-style pines (segmented trunks + flattened canopy pads). - A flattened clearing on the hill flank for the pagoda. - Terrain shader: granite rock on steep slopes (speckled, darker wet band just above the waterline, algae-dark below it), sand with a wet line, darker wet intertidal sand below the high-tide mark, moss/grass on the hill and in patches on the terrace, snow on upward-facing surfaces in winter, procedural animated caustics under water. CPU-baked horizon AO per vertex plus canopy-cover darkening. ARCHITECTURE (merge everything into one vertex-colored mesh + one emissive "glow" mesh; write a small Builder that adds boxes/cylinders/spheres/custom geometry with a color and a transform, then mergeGeometries) - Ryōbu-style torii standing in the bay on the axis of the shrine (~1.9 tall): vermilion tapered main pillars with black base sheaths, four supporting sode-bashira legs with black caps and two connecting beams each, nuki tie beam, central strut with a dark plaque, shimaki, and a curved kasagi (extruded shape with upturned ends) with a black top layer. Pillars must end inside the shimaki, not poke through the kasagi. - Shrine on stilts over the tidal flat: plank deck (with plank-gap strips and dark edge beams) on a grid of wooden stilts reaching the seabed; a main hall and a smaller front hall (white walls, vermilion posts and tie beams, shoji-style front panels = glow panels behind a thin dark lattice), a lower front stage with vermilion railings, and two roofed vermilion corridors on stilts running sideways then back to the shore. - Roofs: a hip-roof generator with a concave profile and lifted eave corners (top surface dark cypress-bark brown, warm wood underside, pale fascia trim, black ridge cap). - A five-storey pagoda on the hill clearing: stone plinth, white walls with vermilion posts, bracket layer, flared roofs decreasing in size, bronze finial with rings. - Stone tōrō lanterns on the terrace and on the stage (hexagonal base, post, firebox with emissive windows, small roof, jewel). VEGETATION - ~4–5k canopy blobs (InstancedMesh of icospheres with vertex-noise displacement + fragment bump), clustered 2–4 per tree, per-instance AO from neighbour occlusion, brighter tops. - Four kinds via an instance attribute: broadleaf, cherry, maple, pine (flattened pads). Cherries cluster lower on the hill and as 5 feature trees with visible trunks on the terrace; pines dominate the summit and the headlands. - Colors come from per-kind dark/light palette uniforms that the JS blends across seasons. SEASONS (cyclic 0..4 = spring, summer, autumn, winter; animated transition from a dock button) - Spring: pink sakura, falling petals. Summer: lush green, no particles. Autumn: red maples, orange/yellow broadleaf, falling maple leaves. Winter: bare-ish brown deciduous blobs shrunk ~38%, snow on canopy tops, roofs, decks, rocks and ground; snowfall that melts instantly on the water. WATER (realistic, not jelly) - Pipeline: opaque scene → MSAA HalfFloat target with DepthTexture; copy to a second target, then draw the water with a custom ShaderMaterial doing a manual depth test; then floating particles; final fullscreen pass with ACES tone mapping, sRGB, subtle tilt-shift. Transparent canvas over the CSS background. - Color from real thickness: reconstruct the depth behind each water pixel, Beer–Lambert absorption toward a deep scatter color derived from the user's water color (pale over the flats, blue in the deep; side walls get extra path length so they read as a water volume). - Screen-space refraction, Fresnel sky reflection, sun glints from fine animated detail normals. - Screen-space reflections (~26 ray-march steps against the depth buffer, fewer on mobile) so the torii, shrine and lit lanterns reflect in the water. - Ripples: GPU wave equation on a 256×256 HalfFloat ping-pong target, fixed 60 Hz steps, land-mask texture so waves reflect off the shore. Cursor movement injects capsule drops along its path; a click makes a splash. - Shore foam only where the terrain is near the water level AND gently sloped (no white outlines around cliffs, stilts or the torii pillars); foam band width scaled by slope; broken by noise. - Tide: a dock toggle animates between high tide (0) and low tide (-0.55): the water block's rim moves and its sides stretch; at low tide the whole flat is exposed and the torii stands on wet sand. PARTICLES (petals / leaves / snow, ~700 instanced quads, CPU-simulated) - Spawn from cherry blobs (spring), deciduous blobs (autumn) or the sky (winter); flutter while falling; a gusting wind blows from the island toward the bay so they reach the water. - Landing: on water they become floating (vertex shader lifts them by the same ripple + wave height as the water), drift slowly, get pushed by the cursor's movement and blown away by click splashes, strand when the tide drops, re-float when it rises; on land they rest and fade. - Shapes drawn in the fragment shader: notched petal, five-lobed maple leaf, soft snow disc. Manual depth test against the scene depth. KOI - 7 koi (lathe body + forked fan tail + pectoral fins, merged), InstancedMesh with a swimming sway in the vertex shader and procedural patterns per type (kohaku, sanke, showa, ogon, plain orange). They wander, steer away from shallow water and the block walls, and flee the cursor and splashes. Rendered under the water so they are refracted and tinted. TIME OF DAY (slider, shown as a clock from 11:00 to ~19:10) - Sun elevation, color and intensity, hemisphere colors, and the water's sky reflection shift from noon to golden hour; towards dusk the shoji panels and lanterns glow (emissive) and three warm point lights light the shrine, the stage and the torii. UI (editorial, minimal, English) Brand "shiosai°" with a small torii mark, headline "A gate that / stands in the sea.", eyebrow "Shrine and tide, in miniature", a vertical caption "A study of tide and seasons", a location label "Shrine Cove · 34°16′ N · 132°19′ E", a floating pill dock (reset, season cycle with the current season name, High tide / Low tide toggle, Tune, fullscreen), hints and an adaptive FPS + "Season · time" readout in the footer, a glassy settings panel (season, time of day, falling petals; water color, tide level, wave height, ripple strength, clarity, caustics; sun azimuth, tilt-shift), and a "How it's made" card. Vermilion accent, light and dark themes via CSS tokens, responsive to 390 px (panel becomes a bottom sheet), prefers-reduced-motion respected, adaptive pixel ratio and a lighter mode for touch devices. Intro: the water fills the block while the camera eases in. ``` ☆ Found this useful? [Star this repo to keep it handy for your next project](https://github.com/LeaddeOpenLab/awesome-opus-5-5-video-prompts). ## What you need - **Inputs:** User inputs not specified by the author - **Tools:** Three.js ## How to try it Copy the prompt into your Opus coding agent, supply the listed inputs, and follow the creator’s tool setup. Ask the agent to report how to preview or render the result and where the output was saved. Repository reproduction: **not_tested**. The preview is the creator’s result.

# Interactive 3D Squishy Toast Memory Foam Simulation ![Preview by @semichenkko](<../data/gifs/2110015093190570491.gif>) By [@semichenkko]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — single self-contained HTML file: Specify one HTML deliverable for easy browser playback; still check whether the implementation loads external dependencies. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build "Squishy Toast" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): an interactive 3D slice of slow-rise memory foam bread you can press, poke, stretch and squash. The toast - A real bread silhouette: square body, rounded "muffin top" crown, soft beveled edges - Crumb face: warm cream color, procedural pores of varied size with highlights and a bump map, a toasted golden edge fading in toward the center - Crust: golden-brown with subtle grain and a light sheen - Lies flat on a white surface at a 3/4 angle with a soft baked contact shadow Physics (this is the whole point - it must feel like foam, not geometry) - Densely tessellated mesh deformed per vertex every frame, normals recomputed - Press and hold: a smooth gaussian dent, crumb bulges outward around the rim, the bottom stays planted on the table - Release: the dent rises back slowly and exponentially, like memory foam, with no instant snap. A faint elastic ripple runs across the crumb after release - Several dents can coexist, each recovering on its own - Grab the crust and pull: the bread stretches elastically, thins as it stretches, then springs back with a damped wobble - Palm squash: the whole slice flattens and barrel-bulges at mid-height, then breathes back up - Drop: lift and release, squash-and-stretch on impact, small decaying bounce Flavors - Butter, strawberry jam (glossy clearcoat, deeper color), avocado (mashed texture). The spread sits on the crumb, leaves a crust rim and deforms with the bread UI - Editorial product-page style on a white background. Large italic serif title "Squishy / Toast.", a short subtitle, a minimal card on the right with flavor swatches, a softness slider (controls dent size and recovery time), a live "Rise" meter and a "Fresh slice" reset button - A subtle circular cursor that shrinks while pressing - ACES tone mapping, soft key and rim lights, environment reflections. Smooth 60fps ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Interactive 3D Snow Globe Comparison ![Preview by @shmopixbzn](<../data/gifs/2110057151171338656.gif>) By [@shmopixbzn]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — every shake leaves a lasting, softly accumulating snowfall: Require snow to accumulate after each shake so interaction changes scene state instead of replaying an effect. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build "Snow Globe": a premium interactive 3D snow globe holding a tiny winter village, where every shake leaves a lasting, softly accumulating snowfall. The emotional goal is the hush after shaking a real snow globe: "I want to shake it again and watch it settle." ART DIRECTION A heavy glass sphere rests on a turned walnut base on a warm linen tabletop. Inside: three cottages with steep roofs, a small chapel, a cluster of pines, a frozen pond and a lamppost. Use a palette of cream, frosted blue, pine green, brick red and warm window amber. The glass should feel real: subtle refraction at the edges, a soft window-shaped highlight, a faint reflection of the room. Snow flakes are small, slightly irregular discs, not uniform dots. Accumulated snow is soft, rounded and matte. CORE INTERACTION Drag the globe to tilt and shake it. Fast motion lifts settled snow into a swirling cloud. Release to let the snow drift and settle. Repeated shakes redistribute snow; gentle ones lift only the top layer. The globe must follow the pointer closely, with a slight weighty lag. On phones, optional device-motion shaking after explicit permission. THE SETTLING Snow inherits the swirl of the liquid: it keeps circling, slows, and falls in lazy spirals. It accumulates as visible layers on roofs, branches, the lamppost cap and the pond. Thick snow slides off steep roofs in small clumps. The village lights glow brighter as the snow quiets. Avoid snow passing through objects, sudden popping into place, or flat uniform coverage. SOUND AND ATMOSPHERE Optional sound: a soft liquid slosh linked to shake velocity, a faint glassy shimmer as snow falls, and a very distant chapel bell when everything has settled. Audio starts only after explicit activation. The scene must feel complete in silence. TECHNICAL APPROACH Use Three.js. Simulate the liquid as a simple damped swirl field driven by globe velocity. Store accumulation in a heightfield or per-surface snow map so it persists and builds. Keep the particle count modest and stable; reuse particles instead of creating new ones. Keep the camera stationary while shaking; allow a restrained orbit when idle. PRESENTATION Show "Snow Globe", the hint "Shake gently. Watch it settle.", and discreet reset and sound controls. Start with a light snowfall already drifting down so the scene is alive on arrival. No introduction modal. DELIVERY AND PRIORITIES Deliver a complete runnable browser experience with procedural geometry and textures and mouse/touch support. First perfect the shake-and-settle feel, then accumulation, then glass rendering and small details. Verify repeated shakes, full settling, reset, and stable performance on mobile. Include setup instructions. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # Three.js Tesla-Style Electric Motor 40-Second Educational 3D Animation ![Preview by @rubenssoto_ai](<../data/gifs/2110065587279798719.gif>) By [@rubenssoto_ai]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — 1920x1080: Set aspect ratio or resolution before composing the scene to avoid cropping after export. ## Prompt (English) ```text Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works. The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS. Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds. Final output: Exact duration: 40.0 seconds Resolution: 1920x1080 Aspect ratio: 16:9 Frame rate: 30 FPS Total frames: 1200 High-quality anti-aliasing High-resolution textures Smooth deterministic animation Extremely realistic visual quality The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial. Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding. FIXED TIMELINE 0–5 seconds — Hero introduction Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment. Use: cinematic lighting realistic brushed aluminum copper steel magnets insulation bearings realistic reflections ambient occlusion realistic shadows subtle depth of field Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor. During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure. 5–11 seconds — Internal components Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components. Clearly show: stator copper windings rotor permanent magnets motor shaft bearings housing cooling channels electrical connections Highlight the important components one at a time. Use floating labels with short technical names. Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent. 11–19 seconds — Exploded view Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation. Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis. Include: outer housing front cover rear cover bearings shaft rotor core rotor magnets stator core copper windings cooling components seals electrical connectors fasteners Keep every component perfectly aligned. The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs. Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components. Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor. 19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation Finish reassembling the motor. Explain how electricity creates rotation. Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings. Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils. Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects. Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor. Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion. The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate. Display these short explanations: "Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field." "The magnetic field interacts with the rotor." "This interaction generates torque." 28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor. Visualize: magnetic north and south poles rotating stator magnetic field rotor magnetic field electric current direction torque direction rotor rotation direction Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees. Then visualize the complete energy conversion process: Electrical energy → stator current → rotating magnetic field → electromagnetic torque → rotor rotation → mechanical output through the shaft. Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow. 34–38 seconds — High-speed operation Show the motor operating at high RPM. The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary. Add subtle motion blur. Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths. Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings. 38–40 seconds — Final hero shot Transition back to the fully assembled motor. Show a slow cinematic rotation. Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside. Finish with the text: "Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation" The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds. VISUAL QUALITY The animation should be: photorealistic cinematic technically believable futuristic premium educational clean and uncluttered Avoid cartoon styling. Use realistic: machining details bolts screws copper winding geometry segmented magnets bearing geometry cooling channels metallic surfaces manufacturing details Use physically based materials with: metallic properties roughness variation normal maps realistic reflections subtle surface imperfections CAMERA Use only smooth cinematic camera movement: slow orbit shots macro close-ups controlled dolly-ins exploded-view fly-throughs cross-section shots internal motor views Avoid: shaky camera movement sudden cuts excessive zooming unrealistic camera acceleration ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS All transitions must be smooth and deliberate. The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights. All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion. Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized. The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems. ``` ☆ Found this useful? A single Japanese vending machine standing alone on a rainy Tokyo street at night, presented as a small floating diorama. It is part of a series of minimal "Night Tokyo" miniatures, so the look matters more than the feature count: one object, rich materials, light and motion you want to keep watching. ## Deliverable - One self-contained `index.html` in the current folder. Open it and it works: no build step, no server-only features. - Three.js only, loaded from a CDN via an import map with an exact pinned version. Official Three.js addons (postprocessing, controls, etc.) are fine. No other libraries. - No external assets: no image textures, models, fonts or audio files. Everything is procedural (geometry, canvas textures, shaders, Web Audio). ## The scene - A cut-out slab of street (about 3×3 m) floating in darkness: wet asphalt with puddles and a strip of curb/sidewalk. The cut edges show a cross-section (asphalt layers, maybe a drain). This is the key shot. - Palette: deep blue-black night, warm white machine light, a few saturated accents from the drinks and buttons. Gummy Bears - classic gummy bear silhouette: round head with two ears, short muzzle, chubby body, stubby arms and legs, small molded eyes and nose - each part smoothly melting into the next - build body as implicit surfaces (metaballs / marching cubes), not separate spheres - Material: realistic gummy candy. Translucent with transmission and refraction, color light absorption deeper in thick parts, glossy lacquer with sharp highlights - Colors: cherry red, orange, lemon yellow, apple green, clear pineapple - soft colored shadow under each bear, tinted by the bear's own color. Physics (this is the whole point - must feel like jelly, not plastic) - each bear is a soft body: mass points for head, ears, muzzle, body, belly, hands, and feet connected via volume-preserving shape matching - limbs and neck rendered as stretchable chains between points that thin when pulled - grab any part and pull: it stretches like rubber, the rest of the bear tilts along, snaps back with damped wobble on release - pull head upward: neck stretches, body follows, releases into squash and jump - press head downward: bear squashes like a pancake, bulges laterally, springs back up - throw a bear: it flies, squashes on landing, bounces, and shoves other bears - bears collide with each other, never pass through - idle bears do small random hops with squash and stretch - "Pour more bears" drops a handful from above into a wobbly, jiggling pile. UI - editorial product page style, white background. Large italic serif header "Gummy / Bears.", a short subhead, a minimalist card on the right with flavor swatches, a wobble slider, live "Stretch" and "Bounce" readouts, and a "Pour more bears" button - a subtle circular cursor that expands on grab - ACES tone mapping, environment reflections, soft key and rim lighting. Smooth 60fps. ``` ☆ Found this useful? # One-Tap Flying Mobile Game in HTML5 Canvas ![Preview by @bytwize](<../data/gifs/2110233825007845872.gif>) By [@bytwize]() · **Prompt disclosure:** full_original > [!TIP] > **💡 Pro Tip** — No external libraries: Exclude external dependencies to reduce failures caused by missing assets, libraries or network requests. ## Prompt (English) ```text Build a polished mobile game I can play in my phone's browser. Concept: a one-tap flying game in the spirit of Flappy Bird, with its own original character, art and name. Tap to flap, gravity pulls you down, fly through the gaps between obstacles. Every gap you pass is +1 point. Hit anything and it's game over. Requirements: - One file: index.html with all HTML, CSS and JavaScript inline. No external libraries, images, fonts or audio files. Draw everything in code and make sounds with the Web Audio API. - Built for phones in portrait. Fill the screen, respect safe areas, stay crisp on high-DPI screens. Tap anywhere to flap; also support mouse click and the space bar for desktop testing. No scrolling, zooming or text selection while playing. - Screens: a start screen with the game's name and a "tap to start" hint, the game, and a game over screen with the score, the best score (saved in localStorage) and a restart button. - Game feel: smooth motion that doesn't depend on frame rate, a character that tilts with its speed, a flap animation, parallax background layers, particles on flap and crash, a small screen shake on crash, and a short vibration on crash where the browser supports it. - Difficulty: start forgiving, then slowly narrow the gaps and speed up as the score grows. - Sound: flap, point and crash sounds, plus a mute toggle. Start audio only after the first tap. - Polish: one consistent art style and color palette, a readable score at the top, nothing under the notch or the home bar. When you're done, check that the game actually works and fix anything that's broken. Then tell me in a few lines what you built and how to run it. ``` ☆ Found this useful?
